  Readable gloss: "Derived from the root idea of extending or stretching out, this noun covers several concrete meanings unified by the concept of measured extent. Most frequently it denotes a garment or military tunic — the robe Ehud concealed his dagger beneath (Judg 3:16) or the armor Saul dressed David in (1 Sam 17:38). Spanish 'túnica' and German 'Gewand' both capture the formal outer-garment sense. In Jeremiah 13:25 it means an allotted measure or portion, while in Judges 5:10 it likely refers to richly dyed saddle-blankets or carpets spread for sitting."

SENSES:
  Sense 1: "garment, robe, clothing"
    Enriched: The most common use, denoting an article of clothing — typically a tunic or outer robe. Multilingual evidence converges strongly: English 'garments,' Spanish 'túnica/ropa,' French 'vêtement,' and German 'Gewand/Mantel' all point to a wearable outer garment rather than underclothing.
    Existing Spanish translations: como-su-vestido, su-ropa, su-túnica, vestidura-suya-de, vestiduras-suyas, y-sus-vestidos, y-vestiduras-suyas
  Sense 2: "stature, tallness"

    Existing Spanish translations: (de-contención), [de-contención]
  Sense 3: "measure, dimension"
    Enriched: The abstract sense of measure, dimension, or apportioned quantity. In Job 11:9 it describes the immeasurable extent of God's wisdom, and in Jeremiah 13:25 the 'portion of your measures' — the allotted share assigned to unfaithful Judah. Spanish 'medidas' and English 'measure' confirm this quantitative reading.
    Existing Spanish translations: es-su-medida,, medidas-tuyas
  Sense 4: "carpet, spread, saddle-blanket"
    Enriched: A hapax use in Judges 5:10, where it likely refers to richly dyed cloths, carpets, or saddle-blankets spread on donkeys for riding. The context of Deborah's song, addressing those who sit on white donkeys upon 'middîn,' supports this as a luxury textile. Spanish 'tapices' (tapestries) captures the nuance well.
    Existing Spanish translations: tapices
